articles.title: Season of sampling and the relationship of serum 25-hydroxyvitamin D3 with mortality and fracture: A population-based cohort study
articles.author: Hannah L. Brooke
articles.summary: by Karl Michaëlsson, Jonas Höijer, Rikard Landberg, Liisa Byberg, Susanna C. Larsson, Bodil Svennblad, Håkan Melhus, Hannah L. Brooke Background Vitamin D supplementation is widespread, yet randomized trials have not demonstrated convincing benefits for future health.
articles.full_html:
by Karl Michaëlsson, Jonas Höijer, Rikard Landberg, Liisa Byberg, Susanna C. Larsson, Bodil Svennblad, Håkan Melhus, Hannah L. Brooke

Background

Vitamin D supplementation is widespread, yet randomized trials have not demonstrated convincing benefits for future health. We need to better identify individuals with true vitamin D deficiency. We aimed to determine how the season of blood draw affects the relationship of serum 25-hydroxyvitamin D3 (S-25OHD3) with mortality, any fracture, and hip fracture risk to identify target groups for vitamin D supplementation.

Methods and findings

Our analyses utilized two Swedish population-based cohorts: one comprising 5,010 women (average age 68 years) and another including 7,291 women and men (average age 75 years). Baseline S-25OHD3 concentrations were measured using liquid chromatography-tandem mass spectrometry. We ascertained information on fractures and death from nationwide registers. We used proportional hazards regression, by season, to estimate multivariable-adjusted (for age, sex, body mass index, renal and liver function, previous fracture, exercise, bone-specific drug use, calcium intake, comorbidities, and smoking) hazard ratios (HRs) with 95% confidence intervals (CI) for mortality and fractures across S-25OHD3 categories. Over an average follow-up of 11 years, 3,573 participants died, and 3,134 experienced fractures (886 hip fractures). The association of S-25OHD3 with death and fractures differed markedly by season of blood draw. For death, the HR in the lowest (<40 nmol/L) versus highest (>80 nmol/L) S-25OHD3 category was 2.86 (95% CI 2.05,3.99) for individuals with blood draws July–September, but 1.36 (95% CI 1.05,1.77) for individuals with blood draws January–March. The corresponding HRs for any fracture were 1.97 (95% CI 1.35,2.89) (July-September) and 1.16 (95% CI 0.89,1.50) (January-March), and for hip fracture were 2.82 (95% CI 1.40,5.71) (July–September) and 1.47 (95% CI 0.88,2.45) (January–March). These patterns were independent of cohort and sex. The main limitation of the study is the observational design, which precludes direct application of the findings into clinical practice.

Conclusions

Our findings suggest that low S‑25OHD3 levels may be clinically significant only when measured during the sunny season, consistent with a season‑dependent meaning of vitamin D deficiency. These findings raise the possibility that we should consider clinical assessment of vitamin D in summer, offer a potential explanation for null results in supplementation trials, and may guide the targeting of future interventions.
